Newman modularity and modularity maximization (use with extreme caution)

modularity.Rd

Computes generalized Newman–Girvan / Reichardt–Bornholdt modularity \(Q(\gamma)\) and maximizes it via fast native C++23 multilevel Louvain coarsening and fine-grained refinement.

Usage

modularity(graph, blocks, gamma = 1.0, weights = NULL)
maximize_modularity(graph, gamma = 1.0, weights = NULL, nruns = 1L,
                    max_levels = 10L, warn = TRUE)
# S3 method for class 'rgraphtool_modularity_state'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

graph

An rgraphtool_graph object.

blocks

Integer partition vector of length graph_num_vertices(graph) (or a fitted block/modularity state).

gamma

Resolution parameter \(\gamma\) (default 1.0).

weights

Optional edge property name or numeric edge weight vector.

nruns

Number of randomized multilevel Louvain restarts; keeps the highest modularity score.

max_levels

Maximum number of Louvain coarsening passes.

warn

Logical; if TRUE (the default), emits an explicit warning explaining why modularity maximization is statistically unsound.

x

An rgraphtool_modularity_state object.

...

Unused; included for S3 print compatibility.

DANGER: Modularity Maximization Considered Harmful

Using modularity maximization for community detection is almost always a terrible idea. Following graph-tool's upstream documentation, maximize_modularity() is included strictly for comparison and pedagogical purposes and emits an explicit warning by default:

  • Massive overfitting of random noise: Modularity has no statistical regularization or prior penalty on the number of groups. On completely structureless Erdos–Renyi or configuration-model random graphs, maximize_modularity() routinely fabricates spurious partitions with high modularity (\(Q > 0.3\)–\(0.8\)), whereas minimize_blockmodel_dl() rightly infers \(B = 1\).

  • Resolution limit (underfitting): Simultaneously, modularity cannot resolve genuine communities smaller than \(\sim \sqrt{2E}\) edges (Fortunato & Barthelemy 2007), merging distinct small modules in large networks.

  • Inferential alternative: For principled Bayesian community detection—including specifically assortative communities—use minimize_blockmodel_dl(), minimize_nested_blockmodel_dl(), or minimize_pp_blockmodel_dl() instead.

See Tiago P. Peixoto (2023), Descriptive vs. inferential community detection in networks: pitfalls, myths and half-truths (Cambridge University Press) and https://skewed.de/tiago/blog/modularity-harmful.

Value

modularity() returns the scalar modularity \(Q(\gamma)\). maximize_modularity() returns an rgraphtool_modularity_state list containing blocks, modularity, B, gamma, and graph.

Examples

# Illustration of modularity overfitting a completely random Erdos-Renyi graph:
set.seed(42)
g_rand <- random_graph_erdos_renyi(80L, p = 0.06)

# Modularity maximization fabricates spurious groups (and warns!):
mod_fit <- suppressWarnings(maximize_modularity(g_rand))
mod_fit$B
#> [1] 7
mod_fit$modularity
#> [1] 0.4340741

# Principled MDL inference rightly finds B = 1 (no community structure):
sbm_fit <- minimize_blockmodel_dl(g_rand)
length(block_sizes(sbm_fit))
#> [1] 1
